title: SVM, Decision Trees & Random Forests
html:
Three classic classifiers on the Iris dataset (150 flowers, 4 measurements, 3 species) — how they decide, and what each is good at.

Support Vector Machine (SVM)

SVM — finds the boundary that separates the classes with the widest margin. With a kernel such as rbf, the boundary can curve.

ParameterEffect
kernellinear (straight boundary), rbf (curved), poly
CLow = wider margin, tolerates mistakes; high = fits training data tightly (risk of overfitting)
gammaFor rbf: how far one sample's influence reaches — high gamma makes wiggly boundaries
Key point

Using only two features caps the accuracy (0.80). Features matter more than the algorithm — the trees below use all four and score 0.98.

Decision Tree

Decision tree — a flowchart of yes/no questions on the features (“petal length ≤ 2.45?”). Each split is chosen to make the groups as pure as possible, measured by Gini impurity or entropy.

Key point

max_depth limits how many questions deep the tree can go — the main defence against a tree memorising the training data. Draw it with sklearn.tree.plot_tree(model, filled=True).

Random Forest

Random forest — many decision trees, each trained on a random sample of rows and features; they vote. Averaging many noisy trees gives a stronger, more stable model (an ensemble).

SVMDecision treeRandom forest
IdeaWidest-margin boundarySequence of feature questionsMany trees voting
InterpretableLowHigh (you can read the tree)Medium (feature importances)
Scaling featuresNeededNot neededNot needed
Overfitting riskTune C, gammaHigh — limit depthLow
